To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the stress induced leakage current technique can be used to determine the dominant defect generation mechanisms and to determine which defect generation mechanisms are responsible for breakdown.

the stress-induced leakage current (SILC) is the most sensitive probe of the interface traps that control breakdown of ultra thin gate dielectrics and that trap generation in ultra thin gate oxides is dominated by a trap-assisted-tunneling mechanism that is driven by the generation of interface traps.
the stress induced leakage current is the most sensitive and informative technique for studying the trap creation processes and their role in breakdown of ultrathin oxynitride gate dielectrics.

the understanding of the physical processes involved in the generation of defects during the electrical stress of ultra-thin SiO 2 gate oxides.
understanding the physical and chemical processes that occur in SiO 2 gate dielectrics when they are stressed electrically.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
trap generation at the gate dielectric/Si interface is the rate limiting process in the breakdown of ultra thin SiON and SiO 2 gate dielectric.
low voltage stress-induced current measurements provide a powerful tool for understanding breakdown and trap generation in ultra thin gate dielectrics and for optimizing their reliability.
low voltage stress-induced current is the best method to determine the trap generation rate in ultra thin SiON and SiO 2 dielectrics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the low stress-induced leakage current technique provides an excellent probe of interface states and their creation, and that the interface traps are the dominant factor in the breakdown of ultra thin SiON and SiO 2 dielectrics.
trap generation in the SiO2/Si interface is the dominant factor for breakdown of ultra thin SiON dielectritics.
trap generation and breakdown are intimately linked and the trap generation mechanisms and defect structures control the breakdown behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that

trap generation in ultra thin SiON and SiO 2 dielectrics is dominated by interface states, and the stress-induced defect that controls breakdown is a trap that is created in the oxide at the contact interface.
the stress-induced leakage current is not a measure of the interface state density.
the defect that controls the onset of breakdown in ultra thin dielectrics is determined by the dominant trap creation mechanism during stress.
